title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New Goal-Reaching Capabilities

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 12 is assigned to two different figures. Section 4.2 and Appendix A.1 define Figure 12 as the comparison of scaled CRL against SAC, SAC+HER, TD3+HER, GCBC and GCSL across 10 environments ('Scaled CRL (ours) outperforms baselines ... in 8 out of 10 environments'). Section 4.4 and the 'Testing the limits of scale' caption define Figure 12 as the depth-scaling (256/1024 layers) results on the Humanoid maze environments. The same figure number refers to two distinct figures.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4 (Width vs. Depth) vs Appendix B.6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.4 states 'the parameter count scales linearly with width but quadratically with depth', while Appendix B.6 states FLOPs and memory 'scale quadratically with width but only linearly with depth'. For MLPs with L layers of width W the parameter count is ~L*W^2 plus linear terms, i.e. it scales quadratically with width and linearly with depth. The B.6 statement is the correct one; the Section 4.4 claim is inverted, and the two sections directly contradict each other.

Section 4.2 claims 'over 50x gains in humanoid-based tasks' and 'over 20x gains in long-horizon maze tasks such as Ant U4-Maze and Ant U5-Maze'. Table 1 reports Humanoid 42x (530/12.6), Humanoid U-Maze 40x (130/3.2), and Ant U4-Maze exactly 20x (230/11.4). Only Humanoid Big Maze (600x) exceeds 50x, so the text overstates the gains relative to its own table.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4, 'Deep Networks Unlock Batch Size Scaling'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The subsection title and Figure 7 caption assert that deeper networks 'can effectively leverage batch size scaling to achieve further improvements' and that 'deeper networks unlock batch size scaling', whereas the body text states 'Figure 7 shows only marginal or inconsistent improvements from increasing batch size, even for larger depth models' and that 'the overall benefit of batch size scaling remains uncertain'. The title/caption and the body text contradict each other.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 6 caption vs Figure 6 data table
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Figure 6 caption claims coordinated actor+critic scaling yields 'an average 30% improvement over critic-only or actor-only scaling across tasks'. Using the tabulated Critic-Depth x Actor-Depth data, joint (depth 64, 64) vs. the best single-axis scaling gives: Humanoid 718/680 = 5.6%, Ant Big Maze 571/462 = 23.6%, Arm Push Easy 864/817 = 5.7%; the average is ~11.6%, well below the stated 30%.

Figure 1's caption says gains 'range from doubling performance to 50x improvements on Humanoid-based tasks', but Table 1 reports Humanoid Big Maze at 600x and Humanoid at 42x, which is inconsistent with capping the improvement at 50x.

Table 3 lists the wall-clock time for Humanoid U-Maze at Depth 64 as 46.74 +/- 0.04 h, while Table 4 ('Total wall-clock time ... in the Humanoid U-Maze environment') lists Depth 64 as 17.33 +/- 0.003 h. The two tables disagree for the same environment and depth, and the caption gives no explanation (e.g. different training lengths) for the discrepancy.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 (Preliminaries) vs Figure 9 caption / hyperparameter table
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3 defines the critic output as a dot-product similarity f_phi,psi(s,a,g) = phi(s,a)^T psi(g), while the hyperparameter table lists energy_function = L2 and Figure 9 computes Q values via the L2 distance ||phi(s,a) - psi(g)||_2. These are different similarity measures for the same critic, and the discrepancy is never reconciled.

The contribution bullet claims 'more than 20x in half of the environments'. Table 1 improvements are 4.7x, 2.0x, 2.1x, 20x, 50x, 6.9x, 1.7x, 42x, 40x, 600x: strictly more than 20x holds for only 4 of 10 environments; including the exactly-20x Ant U4-Maze gives exactly half, so 'more than 20x' is imprecise.

Section 4.4 states Ant Big Maze has observation dimension 29, but Table 1 places Dim = 29 on the Ant U5-Maze row and leaves the Ant Big Maze row blank; similarly Dim = 268 appears only on the Humanoid U-Maze row while the text attributes 268 to the Humanoid environment.

Humanoid Big Maze's improvement is computed as 40/0.06 = 666.7x, which rounds to approximately 670x or 700x, not the reported 600x. The claimed improvement factor is not consistent with the tabulated mean values.

summary: Verification performed in uncertainty mode (threshold 0.30) with lenient strictness. The paper was segmented into 56 snippets (28 sections, 4 equations, 12 tables, 12 figure captions), triaged, and high-uncertainty snippets routed to specialist verifiers (text, statistical, math, vision, citation). 11 predicted errors were identified. The most serious are a cross-reference collision in which Figure 12 is used for two different figures (Section 4.2/Appendix A.1 baseline comparison vs. Section 4.4 depth-to-1024 scaling), and a direct internal contradiction on parameter-count scaling: Section 4.4 claims parameters scale linearly with width and quadratically with depth, while Appendix B.6 states the opposite (and the correct) scaling, quadratic in width and linear in depth. Additional medium-confidence findings: Section 4.2 overstates improvement factors relative to Table 1 ('over 50x' vs. 42x/40x humanoid results); the 'Deep Networks Unlock Batch Size Scaling' title/caption contradict the body text reporting only marginal or inconsistent batch-size gains; the Figure 6 '30% improvement' claim is not supported by the tabulated actor/critic depth data (~12% average); Table 4's Depth-64 wall-clock for Humanoid U-Maze (17.33h) disagrees with Table 3 (46.74h); the critic is defined via dot-product in Section 3 but evaluated via L2 distance in Figure 9; and several minor numeric/table inconsistencies (improvement rounding, Dim column placement, 'more than 20x in half of the environments'). The Neumann & Gros (2022) scaling-laws citation was checked externally and is a real, correctly attributed paper (arXiv:2210.00849), so no citation error is reported there. Two findings exceed the high-confidence threshold (0.85), so the paper requires correction.
